\section{Related Work}
\label{sec-relatedwork} 

\subsection{Data Dependence}

The data dependence test 
\cite{optimizing-compilers,yu2012fast,data-depend-83} targets two array references and at least one of them is a write. On the contrary, redundant computation means two or more expressions performing the same operation on the same array elements (or the same values). Thus, the redundancy detection focuses on reads. However, this is not an essential difference. The dependence techniques can also be applied to find two array reads to the same memory address.

The essential differences between the data dependence test and the computation redundancy elimination are three-fold.
First, the dependence test seeks to 
check whether there is at least one iteration that the two references access the same memory address. 
However, the redundancy elimination in loops only targets a large number
of common computations.
Second, the practical general dependence test technique is often conservative in the sense that it may report a false dependence but must report all real data dependence.
However, as an optimization technique, the redundancy elimination should
ensure a potential performance improvement.
Finally, the data dependence test focuses on array references,
while the computation redundancy targets expressions.
Therefore, it needs a new method to determine the redundancy 
between two data reuses and between two expressions.
 



\subsection{Redundancy Elimination}




Two classic redundancy elimination techniques for the scalar computation
are the value numbering and common subexpression elimination (CSE)~\cite{valuenumber,constant-propagation,common-subexpr-elim}.
The key idea underlying both methods is to record the identification of the operands.
The value numbering assigns the same number to the variables that share the same value,
while CSE utilizes the available expression in the data-flow analysis to recognize the operand change.
However, they only target scalar variables.



Cooper et al \cite{Cooper+:pact08} propose the enhanced scalar replacement (ESR), the seminal redundancy elimination method for loops. ESR employs two classic optimization techniques, value numbering and classic scalar replacement (CSR)~\cite{csr}.
ESR has the following disadvantages.
First, ESR only considers the recomputation across the innermost loop. It fails to discover all redundancies. Second, ESR incorporates the scalar replacement, which relies on advanced data dependence analysis. However, data dependence is not suitable for redundancy detection, which requires a more precise definition and method. Third, ESR is a two-step method that separates the name partition and index alignment. It will compare the unnecessary expressions that are not redundant. Fourth, the affinity graph in ESR fails to discover redundant computations of the arrays within the same name partition. Finally, ESR seeks to find the maximal computation redundancy in a single execution of their algorithm. However, as the example
in Section~\ref{sec-motivation} demonstrates, the computation redundancy may exhibit a hierarchical property. 


Deitz et al~\cite{Deitz+:ics01}
proposed array subexpression elimination (ASE)
for sum-of-product array expressions.
Like ESR, it also aims to eliminate the redundancies over the innermost loop dimension. 
ASE depends on a specific framework called neighborhood tablet 
to search the redundancy.
Basu et al~\cite{Basu+:ipdps15} targeted stencil computations
and designed a specific optimization scheme. 
It employs extra arrays to 
buffer partial sums within the
leading plane of the whole iteration space.
However, it only focuses on simple stencils and 
reduces redundant computations effectively for 
stencils with symmetric coefficients.
These methods lack generality 
and fail to process complex subexpressions, e.g. $ a(i) * c (j,k)$.
Chi and Cong \cite{Chi.Cong:dac20} developed
heuristic search–based reuse (HSBR)
for stencil computations. They did observe the conflict between expressions
but did not formalize it as we do.


RCE (redundant computation elimination) \cite{Yuan+:ica3pp16}
is able to explore redundancies with temporal locality for stencils
but their search algorithm compares all possible expressions
and incurs high overhead.
This scheme is also utilized by the
loop-carried CSE method proposed in \cite{Kronawitter+:ica3pp16}.
On the contrary, our method assigns each expression
a hash number and redundancies can be easily
identified by extracting expressions with the same hash number.
Wen et al \cite{Wen+:pact15} 
implemented a profiler to
pinpoint redundant computations by runtime checking. It finds redundancies in
several stencil computations and eliminates them by hand-written optimizations

Redundancy elimination, as well as many other compiler optimizations, such as loop transformation, memory access optimization and vectorization, relies on the results of aliasing analysis~\cite{alias-analysis, interprocedual-alias}. 
Alias analysis disambiguates memory references, primarily serving for the legality verification or candidate selection. 
For example, existing work like ESR~\cite{Cooper+:pact08} selects the redundancy candidates using the results of data dependence analysis which implicitly incorporates alias analysis. 
Thus, alias analysis is orthogonal to these optimizations to some extent.
Furthermore, existing aliasing analysis techniques are powerful but not panaceas.
Other mechanisms such as the \texttt{restrict} keyword, \texttt{-fno-alias} compiler option, and \texttt{\#pragma ivdep} directive are provided to enable more aggressive optimizations.
Therefore, in this paper, RACE focuses on the detection technique of redundancies, instead of directly incorporating alias analysis.


\section{Redundancy Identification}
\label{sec:identification}


This section first limits the scope of this paper.
Then, the following two parts describe the two-level redundancy identification scheme.
The first level focuses on data sharing among array references. 
Each array reference is assigned with an identification to determine
its reference pattern.
Array references with the same identification value
may access a sufficiently large set of common array elements.
The second level identifies the redundancies among expressions.
As mentioned before, the proposed method detects redundancies
hierarchically.
Thus, the second identification only focuses on 
expressions with two operands, and larger expressions will be processed iteratively.
With this two-level hash mechanism, 
RACE achieves linear-time redundancy detection, 
while all previous methods require direct pair-wise comparisons between expressions which incurs a quadratic time complexity.
The computation redundancy can be easily discovered by grouping the 
expressions with the same identification value
in linear time.


\subsection{Target}

This paper describes our work using perfectly nested loops, where
all the statements are inside the innermost loop.
The experiment was also conducted on perfectly nested loops with no branch statement inside the loop.
However, the design is easy to be extended
and our implementation is able to handle imperfectly nested loops.

RACE eliminates redundant computations in unmodified arrays within the loop.
Each candidate expression considered in the algorithm
involves arithmetic operations 
on scalar or array variables.
RACE targets array references of the form
$A[a_1i_{s_1}+b_1]\dots[a_ni_{s_n}+b_n]$, where $s_k$ is a loop level number ranking from the outermost loop to the innermost,
$1\leqslant s_k\leqslant m$, $m$ is the nesting depth of the loop structure, $i_{s_k}$ is a loop index, $a_k$ and $b_k$ are constants.
For all the array references in the above POP example in Figure~\ref{fig-pop1},
we have $s_1=2$ and 
$s_2=1$, and 
$i_{s_1}=i$ and $i_{s_2}=j$.
This form covers most loop nests in real-world applications.
For the applications used in the evaluation of this work, over 95\% of array accesses in loops conform to this pattern.
Scalars are considered zero-dimensional array references. 
Function calls such as $\sin$ and $\cos$ can be interpreted as binary operators $\copyright$, where the function name is treated as a scalar variable.
For example, $\cos(ulat(1,j-1))$ can be viewed as a binary expression $\cos \copyright ulat(1,j-1)$, where $\cos$ and $\ulat(1,j-1)$ are the left and right operands.



\subsection{Reference Pattern Identification ($\rpi$)}


To recognize the redundancy among expressions, the reuse of array references needs to be analyzed. As explained above, the data dependence techniques test whether two array references may access at least the same array element. However, the redundancy elimination of array computations requires the reference of a sufficiently large set of common array elements.

In particular, this paper only considers the redundancy among array references with the same \emph{reference pattern} in the \emph{data space} of an array. The data space of an $n$-dimensional array $A$ is
a finite subset of
$\mathbb{Z}^n$ consisting of
all the accessible n-dimensional elements,
but we regard the data space
as the entire infinite space $\mathbb{Z}^n$
since we consider the pattern rather than a
specific range.
Two array references share the same reference pattern if they access the same infinite sub-lattice in the data space when the range of all loop indices is $\mathbb{Z}$. 
For example, $A[i][j]$ and $A[i+1][j-1]$ have the same reference pattern since they both touch all the lattice points in the data space
of $A$, $\{(i,j)\mid i, j \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, while the reference lattices of $A[2i]$ and $A[2i+1]$ are disjoint. $A[2i]$ and $A[3i]$ access partial common lattice points,
$\{6i\mid i \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.


Formally, 
the infinite sub-lattice of $A[a_1i_{s_1}+b_1]\dots[a_ni_{s_n}+b_n]$
is defined by
$\mathcal{L}(B,b) = \{\textit{B}x + b \mid x=(i_1,\dots, i_m)\in \mathbb{Z}^m\}$, where $m$ is the nesting depth of the loop structure,
$n$ is the dimension of the array $A$,
$B$ is a matrix of size $n\times m$, $B_{k,s_k} = a_k$  and all other elements are 0, $b$ is a vector of size $n$ and its $k$-th component is $b_k$.



We now define the reference pattern identification ($\rpi$) to help recognizing the array references with the same reference pattern. Notice that $i_k$ determines the dimension axis, $B_{n\times m}$ identifies the lattice basis and $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ is the offset of the origin. It is easy to see that if two references share the same reference pattern, their index list (dimension axis) $\{i_{s_1},\dots,i_{s_n}\}$ must be the same. 
It is also straightforward to see that the coefficient list $\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}$ must be the same. For example, the point lattices of $A[2i]$ and $A[3i]$ are different.

The last information in $\rpi$ is the offset vector $b$. 
According to the above two requirements, two lattices
$\mathcal{L}(B,b)$ and $\mathcal{L}(B',b')$ 
can be equal only if 
$B=B'$. Furthermore,
$\mathcal{L}(B,b) = \mathcal{L}(B,b')$ if and only if
$b-b' \in \mathcal{L}(B,0)$,
i.e. $Bx=b-b'$ has an integral solution.

Given two potential references $A[a_1i_{s_1}+b_1]\dots[a_ni_{s_n}+b_n]$ and $A[a_1i_{s_1}+b_1']\dots[a_ni_{s_n}+b_n']$.
If a loop index $i_{s_k}=i$ appears only once in the array reference, 
$a_ki = b_k-b_k'$ has an integral solution if and only if
$b_k \bmod a_k = b_k' \bmod a_k$.
Thus $\rpi$ can incorporate 
$b_k \bmod a_k$.
For example, $A[2i]$ and $A[2i+2]$ have the same $\rpi$. 
If there are multiple appearances of $i$, the successive deltas (differences) must also be equal. 
Assume $i_{s_k}=i_{s_j}=i$,
the two equations 
$a_k i = b_k - b_k'$ and 
$a_j i = b_j - b_j'$
must have the same integral solution.
In addition to $b_k \bmod a_k = b_k' \bmod a_k$ for the first equation,
it is easy to obtain that the necessary and sufficient condition for the second equation is that $b_k/a_k - b_j/a_j$
and $b_k'/a_k - b_j'/a_j$
must  be equal.
For example, the two references $A[2i+1][3i+2]$ and $A[2i+3][3i+5]$ have the same delta value $2/3-1/2=5/3-3/2=1/6$ for $i$.
Thus they access the same infinite
sub-lattice.


Algorithm~\ref{alg:rpi} shows the pseudo-code extracting the information for $\rpi$. The descriptions of the used variables are given below:
$\mathit{indexList}$ and $\mathit{indexCoef}$ store the loop index variables and their corresponding coefficients in the order they appear.
$\mathit{firstIndexOffset}$ stores the normalized offset of each loop index variable when it first appears. It is used to compute $\mathit{indexDelta}$ which contains the successive deltas of the same loop index variable. For the calculation of $\mathit{indexDelta}$, it keeps the rational results 
in the irreducible fraction form. 
If a loop index is missing, i.e. $a_k = 0$, it appends a virtual loop level $0$ and the corresponding constant $b_k$ must be added to the coefficient list. For example, $A[i][1]$ and $A[i][2]$ do not share common elements and the coefficients $1$ and $2$ are the only identifications in this dimension. 
Let $x.\mathit{name}$ denotes the name of the array reference $x$.
Put it all together, $\rpi$ is formulated as follows:


$$\rpi(x) = \hash(x.\mathit{name},x.\mathit{indexList},x.\mathit{indexCoef},x.\mathit{indexDelta})$$


\begin{algorithm}[h]
    \caption{Calculating information for $\rpi$}
    \label{alg:rpi}
    \SetKwInOut{Input}{input}
    \SetKwInOut{Output}{output}
    \Input{An array reference $x=A[a_1 i_{s_1} + b_1]\dots[a_n i_{s_n} + b_n]$}
    \Output{$\mathit{indexList},\mathit{indexCoef},\mathit{indexDelta},\mathit{firstIndexOffset}$ of $x$}
    \tcp{$x.\mathit{indexList}$ and $x.\mathit{indexCoef}$ are lists}
    \tcp{$x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}$ is an array of rationals}
    \tcp{$x.\mathit{indexDelta}$ is an array of lists of rationals}

    
    $x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[1\dots m] = \infty$\; 
    \For{$k \gets 1$ \KwTo $n$}{
        \uIf{$a_k \neq 0$}{
            $x.\mathit{indexList}.$append$(s_k)$\;
            $x.\mathit{indexCoef}.$append$(a_k)$\;
            \uIf{$x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[s_k] = \infty$}{
                $x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[s_k] = b_k/a_k$\;
                $x.\mathit{indexDelta}[s_k]$.append($b_k \bmod a_k$)\;
            } \Else{
                $x.\mathit{indexDelta}[s_k]$.append($b_k/a_k - x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[s_k]$) \;
            }
        } \Else{
            $x.\mathit{indexList}.$append$(0)$\; 
            $x.\mathit{indexCoef}$.append($b_k$) \;
        }
    }
\end{algorithm}



\subsection{Expression Redundancy Identification ($\eri$)}



\begin{algorithm}[h]
    \caption{Calculating information for $\eri$}
    \label{alg:eri}
    \SetKwInOut{Input}{input}
    \SetKwInOut{Output}{output}
    \Input{An expression $e=x\oplus y$}
    \Output{$\mathit{exprDelta}$ of $e$}
    \tcp{$e.\mathit{exprDelta}$ is an array of rationals}
    $e.\mathit{exprDelta}[1\dots m] = \infty,$ \;
    \For{$s_k \in \{x.\mathit{indexList}\} \cap \{y.\mathit{indexList}\} - \{0\}$}{
            $e.\mathit{exprDelta}[s_k] = x.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[s_k] - y.\mathit{firstIndexOffset}[s_k]$\;
    }
\end{algorithm}


With $\rpi$ of each operand, we can define the expression redundancy identification ($\eri$) to recognize expressions with redundant computations. If one of the operands is scalar, its $\rpi$ just hashes the name. 
Otherwise, it must align the offsets of each loop variable.
For example, the two expressions $e=A[i]+B[i]$ and $e'=A[i+1]+B[i+2]$ are not redundant.
Since $\rpi(A[i])=\rpi(A[i+1])$ and $\rpi(B[i])=\rpi(B[i+2])$ are the same, the $\eri$ cannot
be as simple as the classical value number definition like $vn(e)=\hash(vn(x), \oplus, vn(y))$.
For the loop index $i$, two operands in each expression 
induce another delta value at the expression level.
Algorithm \ref{alg:eri} presents the pseudo-code for calculating 
this information for $\eri$. 
$\mathit{exprDelta}$ stores the delta between the two operands of the expression for each loop index variable.
The formula of $\eri$ for $e=x\oplus y$ is as follows:
$$\eri(e) = \hash(\rpi(x),\oplus,\rpi(y),e.\mathit{exprDelta})$$

For commutative operations such as addition and multiplication, the two operands need to be sorted to recognize the redundancy.
For example, $A[i]+B[i]$ and $B[i+1]+A[i+1]$
are considered as redundant computations.
The two operands can be sorted by their $\mathit{name}$
$A$ and $B$ lexicographically.
If the two operands access the same array,
they are sorted according to their other $\rpi$ information:
$\mathit{indexList}$, $\mathit{indexCoef}$ and $\mathit{indexDelta}$.
Thus, the redundancies between 
$A[i]+A[j]$ and $A[i+1]+A[j+1]$,
$A[i]+A[2i]$ and $A[i+1]+A[2i+2]$,
and $A[i]+A[i+1]$ and $A[i+1]+A[i+2]$
can be found.
Without loss of generality, we assume that the operands in $e=x\oplus y$ are already in order.









\section{Redundancy Elimination on Binary Tree}
\label{sec:detectionbinary}


The two-level scheme simplifies the redundancy detection algorithm, especially working with binary expression trees.
Complex expressions can be handled repeatedly and
the redundancies exhibit a 
hierarchical structure.
Generating the straightforward code is also simple
but it requires a large extra space for auxiliary arrays.
This section presents a technique to reduce their dimensions.


\subsection{Detection Algorithm}

Redundancy elimination stores the intermediate result and reuses it for the same succeeding calculations. Therefore, it can intrinsically guarantee the consistency of the final computing result. Results consistency is usually important for scientific applications that involve floating-point arithmetic operations.
To achieve this, the computing order must be respected.
Thus we first present the detection algorithm working on the high-level intermediate representation (IR), where the computation order is fixed. 

The value numbering works on linear IR, such as the three-address code.
It just requires one sequential traversal of the IR code to find all redundancies.
The reason is that each expression $a=b\oplus c$ can be assigned a number 
used for the following redundancy check,
regardless of whether $b$ and $c$ are redundancies.
However, in the array redundancy detection of $a=b[\dots]\oplus c[\dots]$, 
the $\rpi$ is only defined on array references $b[\dots]$ and $c[\dots]$,
and the $\eri$ can only be computed on $a$.
If there is a following statement $e=a \oplus d[\dots]$,
it cannot check the redundancy of $e$ until $a$
is replaced with a new array $f[\dots]$ storing the redundant value $b[\dots]\oplus c[\dots]$.


To find all redundancies in linear time, 
the detection algorithm of array computations works on the binary expression trees
in a bottom-up scheme, as shown in Algorithm \ref{alg:lineardetection}. 
First, the $\rpi$ values of all the leaves in the expression trees are set to $\infty$.
In each iteration of the do-while loop,
all the leaves are associated with their $\rpi$ values, 
and the expressions whose two sons are leaves are assigned their $\eri$ values.
Then, all the $\eri$ values are compared to find redundancies.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
  \caption{Detection on binary tree}
  \label{alg:lineardetection}
  \SetKwRepeat{Do}{do}{while}
  set $\rpi$ of all leaves to $\infty$ \;
  \Do{$\exists$ a leaf $v$ with $\rpi==\infty$}{
    calculate $\rpi$\ for all leaves with $\rpi==\infty$\;
    calculate $\eri$\ for all binary expressions whose child's $\rpi$ is computed \;
    find redundancies according to all $\eri$ values \;
    allocate new auxiliary arrays for all redundancies as new leaves \;
    replace redundant expressions  to auxiliary array loads with corresponding offsets  \;
    set the $\rpi$ of new leaves to $\infty$ \;
  }
\end{algorithm}

A new array is allocated and precomputed before the loop for each redundant $\eri$,
and it replaces the corresponding operations with auxiliary array references in the expression trees.
These new references must coordinate their subscripts.
To do this, we select one representative expression for each auxiliary array.
For example, $\cos(ulat(i,j))$, $\cos(ulat(i,j-1))$, $\cos(ulat(i-1,j))$ and $\cos(ulat(i-1,j-1))$
in the POP example
are with the same $\eri$ and 
we set the corresponding auxiliary array $aa\_0\_0(i,j)$ to an representative expression,
e.g.  $aa\_0\_0(i,j)=\cos(ulat(i,j))$. Then all these four redundant computations in the expression trees can be replaced with auxiliary array references with coordinated offsets.
Finally, the newly added array references are identified as new leaves whose $\rpi$ values
are set to $\infty$.
The do-while loop repeatedly executes until it finds no more new redundancies (new leaves).
It is easy to see that the algorithm has linear time complexity.



The algorithm detects and organizes the redundancies hierarchically,
as illustrated by the POP example in Section \ref{sec-motivation}.
Except for the first and last one, each iteration of the do-while loop finds new redundant
expressions that have auxiliary arrays as operands, which are added in the previous iteration.
The correctness is due to the reason that redundancies are composable.
Given two expressions $e=x\oplus y\oplus z$ and $e=x'\oplus y' \oplus z'$,
it is easy to see that $e$ and $e'$ are  redundant
if there are redundancies exist between $x\oplus y$ and $x'\oplus y'$, and between $y\oplus z$ and $y'\oplus z'$.


The proposed detection algorithm using $\eri$ can iteratively identify hierarchical redundancies as $\eri$ is composable. 
For example, if $(x\oplus y)\oplus z$ is redundant with $(x'\oplus y')\oplus z'$,
it can be detected after
$x\oplus y$ is first discovered as redundancy and
replaced with an auxiliary array.
The proof is straightforward according to the definitions of $\rpi$ and $\eri$.
The algorithm is also optimal with respect to the array computation,
and all the redundancies from the expressions can be determined.

\emph{Code Generation.}
The expression trees are optimized with auxiliary arrays 
after the execution of Algorithm~\ref{alg:lineardetection}.
The auxiliary arrays will have hierarchical structures as the algorithm is conducted iteratively. A directed acyclic graph is used to represent the dependencies between auxiliary arrays, which is called the dependency graph. Obviously, there is a topological order in the dependence graph. Figure~\ref{fig:dependency-graph} illustrates the dependency graph of auxiliary arrays in POP benchmark. An edge from auxiliary array node $a$ to $b$ means $b$ is used to compute $a$, so the precomputation of $b$ should appear before that of $a$. 
The variables assigned in the original loop are placed on the topmost level.
For each auxiliary array, the representative expression selected in Algorithm \ref{alg:lineardetection},
e.g., $aa\_0\_0(i,j)=\cos(ulat(i,j))$, will not be changed after extraction and is used as the assignment statement in the precompute loop. 

Generating the straightforward code for the auxiliary arrays, i.e., the code on the left of Figure~\ref{fig-pop2}, requires auxiliary arrays' topological order and loop ranges. The topological order determines which array is computed first. The loop range information determines the precompute loop's range. The top nodes $tx,ty,tz$ are in the original loop, and their loop range information is set to the original loop's range, which is $[2,nx][2,ny]$ in this case. With the representative expression, each parent node can pass the reference offsets with its loop range to update the children's loop range. Each node will have its own loop range information computed following a topological order. For example, $aa\_2\_0$ is only used by $tx$ with indices $(i,j)$ and $(i-1,j)$. So $aa\_2\_0$'s range is shifted to $[1,nx][2,ny]$. The loop ranges (e.g. $[1,nx][2,ny]$) and the reference offsets (e.g. $(i-1,j)$) of nodes are shown in the figure.

After the loop ranges of all the auxiliary arrays are determined, the straightforward code can be generated. Firstly, the nodes with the same loop range will be put into the same circle called range circle, which is colored in Figure~\ref{fig:dependency-graph}. For example, $aa\_2\_0, aa\_2\_1, aa\_1\_2$ are in the same circle. To simplify the generated code, auxiliary arrays in the same range circle will be initialized in the same loop. By considering range circles as basic units for code generation, we will get a new graph in which the nodes are range circles. And there is an edge from circle $c_1$ to $c_2$ only if there is an edge from any node in $c_1$ to any node in $c_2$. It is easy to prove that there is a topological order of the range circles. Loops are generated one by one following the topological order of the range circles. The order of the auxiliary arrays in the same circle should follow the topological order of the dependency graph. This will generate the code shown on the left of Figure~\ref{fig-pop2}.

\begin{algorithm}[h]
\DontPrintSemicolon
\KwIn{$\mathit{loop\_insert\_pos}$: Loop insert positions, $G$: Range circle graph}
\SetKwFunction{ArrayContraction}{arrayContraction}
\SetKwProg{Fn}{Function}{:}{}
\SetKw{In}{in}
\Fn{\ArrayContraction{loop\_insert\_pos, G}}{
    \For{circle \In $\mathrm{topologicalOrder}(G)$}{
        \For{insert\_pos \In loop\_insert\_pos}{
          \If{insert\_pos is in the innermost loop}{
            $\mathit{circle.dump}(\mathit{insert\_pos})$\;
            \textbf{break}\;
          }
          \tcp{$insert\_pos.loop$ is the loop subsequent to $insert\_pos$.}
          $loop = insert\_pos.loop$\;
          \tcp{$range\_at$ returns the circle's range on $loop$'s index variable.}
          \uIf{circle.range\_at(loop) doesn't exist}{
            $\mathit{circle.dump}(\mathit{insert\_pos})$\;
            \textbf{break}\;
          }
          \ElseIf{circle.range\_at(loop) $\neq$ loop.range}{
            $\mathit{circle.dumpPrefetch}(\mathit{insert\_pos})$\;
            $\mathit{circle.dumpPipeline}(\mathit{insert\_pos.next})$\;
            \textbf{break}\;
          }
        }
    }
}
\caption{Array Contraction}
\label{alg:arrayContraction}
\end{algorithm}
  

\emph{Array Contraction.}
This simple code allocates a large space for the auxiliary array. However, it is possible to decrease the auxiliary dimensionality and reuse a small array space. 

First, if an auxiliary array has only one parent, it can be replaced by its representative expression without storing the array explicitly. The final optimized code on the right of Figure~\ref{fig-pop2} shows that $aa\_0\_0$ and $aa\_0\_2$ are replaced by $\cos(ulon(i,j))$ and $\sin(ulon(i,j))$, when used by $aa\_1\_0$ and $aa\_1\_1$.

Second, an auxiliary array can be replaced by a scalar if all of its parents are in the same circle with it. If the condition is true, the reference offsets from its parents must be zeros. Otherwise, their range will not be the same. So $aa\_0\_1$ can be replaced by a scalar variable $aa\_0\_1\_i\_j$, which is shown in the right code in Figure~\ref{fig-pop2}.

Third, the dimension of auxiliary arrays can be eliminated or compressed to half-dimension. The right of Figure~\ref{fig:dependency-graph} shows the original loop. The numbers with arrows show different loop insert positions where our precompute loops can be inserted. In the previous discussion, the loops are all inserted into position 0. 
If the references of an auxiliary array have the same offset at $j$ dimension in the original loop, the precompute loop of it can be put into the inner position 1, and the $j$ dimension can be eliminated from the array. 
We consider a range circle as a whole instead of investigating the loop of each single auxiliary array. We can recursively check if a circle can be put into an inner loop. The check starts from the outmost insert position 0. For each range circle, if the corresponding dimension matches the current loop, then this dimension can be eliminated from the auxiliary arrays in the circle. The check continues to the next insert position until it fails.
For example, the orange circle in Figure~\ref{fig:dependency-graph} has the same range as the original loop on $j$, so its $j$ dimension is eliminated and it passes to position 1. The right code in Figure~\ref{fig-pop2} shows that the $j$ dimension of $aa\_2\_0, aa\_2\_1, aa\_1\_2$ is eliminated.

If the range of current checking dimension mismatches, the dimension of the auxiliary array will be reduced to half-dimension. For example, the blue circle's $j$ range $[1,ny]$ is different from the original $[2,ny]$. Instead of leaving the loop to position 0, the range can be split into two parts $[1,1]$ and $[2,ny]$. The $[1,1]$ part is a prefetch loop at position 0, and the other part will enter the $j$ loop at position 1. The range $[1,ny]$'s lower bound is less than the original loop because there are some references $j-1$ to the blue circle. So we can allocate the auxiliary arrays in the blue circle with a smaller memory space $nx*2$ and swap the $j$ index during the loop, which is a pipeline style. We call it a $1.5$ dimension array, which has half-dimension. The formal algorithm is shown in Algorithm~\ref{alg:arrayContraction}. Specifically in this case, the prefetch loop will compute $aa\_1\_0(1 \to nx,j0)$, and position 1 will have a $i$ loop computing $aa\_1\_0(1 \to nx, j1)$. 
Before entering the next $j$ iteration, the old data in $j0$ is discarded, leaving the next $j$ loop to compute $aa\_1\_0(1 \to nx, j1)$ after swapping $j1$ and $j0$. After the circle's loop is split, the arrays in it can't be compressed anymore. But the loop fusion can also be done. If the loops appeared at the same insert position have the same inner range, they can be merged into one loop. Continue the check for other nodes iteratively, until there is nothing to do. The right code in Figure~\ref{fig-pop2} shows that precompute loop of the arrays in the blue circle is split, and the inner loop is merged into the orange circle's $i$ loop. Note that the innermost dimension $i$ is retained to facilitate vectorization.






\subsection{Redundancy Analysis}
\label{subsec:redundancy-analysis}


After identifying the expressions with the same $\eri$ value, these redundant expressions can be replaced with precomputed auxiliary arrays. The range information for each auxiliary array is computed in the dependency graph. The evaluation of the profit gained from the replacement, i.e., the number of arithmetic operations eliminated, is discussed in this section.


Suppose that the auxiliary arrays $aa_1, \dots, aa_m$ appear in the transformed expression trees while the remaining positions are the original tree nodes. Let $cnt(aa_k)$ denote the appearance number of $aa_k$ in the expression trees. For loop ranges, only the difference between the lower and upper bound is considered, which is denoted by $r(i_t)$ for the original loop range at index $i_t$. Let $r(i_t,aa_k)$ denote the precompute loop range of auxiliary array $aa_k$ at index $i_t$. 

The reduction in arithmetic operations is only related to the modified parts of the expression trees. The first step is to calculate the original computational cost of the replaced parts. This can be done by recursively expanding the representative expression of each auxiliary array. Specifically, if the representative expression of $aa_k$ contains $aa_p$, the corresponding part should be replaced by the representative expression of $aa_p$, continuing until all operands are no longer auxiliary arrays. Let the number of arithmetic operations in the expanded representative expression of $aa_k$ be denoted by $ops(aa_k)$. The original computational cost of the positions replaced by the auxiliary arrays in the expression tree can be computed, and combined with the loop range, the total reduction in computations in the original loop after extraction is given by:
\[ori= \prod_{t=1}^n r(i_t) \sum_{k=1}^m ops(aa_k) \cdot cnt(aa_k) \]

However, generating the auxiliary arrays requires precomputation loops. Therefore, the computational cost associated with this additional precomputation must also be accounted for to determine the benefit. Since our $\eri$ method targets binary expressions, each auxiliary array's precompute expression is a binary expression, thus the precomputation cost of the auxiliary arrays is:
\[aft=\sum_{k=1}^m \prod_{t=1}^n r(i_t,aa_k) \]

So the profit gained from the detection algorithm on binary tree is $ori-aft$.

heuristic method for reducing the algorithm complexity and improving the code efficiency
is provided.

\subsection{Tree Flattening}
\label{subsec:flattening}



It may demand the reorganization of expressions to find
redundancies for array computations and even classic scalar calculations
with commutative, associative, and distributive operations.
Consider the two expressions $x+y+z$ and $x+z$.
Compilers may specify a pre-defined order for the former one.
The order can be either $((x+y)+z)$ with the left-associative rule or $(x+(y+z))$
with the right-associative rule, but none of them can
detect the redundancy with $x+z$ unless
the expression is allowed to be reordered by commutative, associative, and even distributive reorganizations.
Note that the commutative law here is not the same as the one used 
in the $\eri$ calculation, where the expressions only have two operands. 

However, to produce consistent results, it is generally illegal to perform the operation
reassociation even for the integral computation.
Take the expression  $x+y+z$  as an example again, 
if $x$ and $z$ are very large positive integers and 
$y$ is a very small negative integer,
$((x+y)+z)$ and $(x+(y+z))$ may produce the correct result
but $((x+z)+y)$ may result in an integer overflow.
Nevertheless, compilers usually provide options to control the expression reorganization
for aggressive optimizations
and leave the decision to users.


Therefore, the implementation of RACE provides several options to control the reassociation scheme.
We describe them by three aggressive levels.
First, if a consistent result is required, 
the reassociation is prohibited
and the linear redundancy detection algorithm described above is employed.
Second, all the parentheses in the source code are respected,
and the reorganization can be only applied inside each parenthesis
which includes more than two operands.
Third, the parenthesis is removed when the operators are 
consistent with the one outside the parenthesis.
Finally, the distributive law is applied to remove more parentheses.
The tree flattening algorithm is trivial according to the aggressive level. 
It simply traverses the original binary tree in a post-order manner and merges the children that have the same operator as the current node after visiting them.

The first three levels are simple. 
However, the distributive law should be applied cautiously. 
It may destroy existing redundancies.
For example, it is obvious that there are two pairs of redundancies in $e=(a[i]+b[i])*(c[i]+d[i])+(a[i+1]+b[i+1])*(c[i+2]+d[i+2])$,
i.e. $\eri(a[i]+b[i])= \eri(a[i+1]+b[i+1])$ and $\eri(c[i]+d[i])=\eri(c[i+2]+d[i+2])$.
However, if the  distributive law is applied, both of the redundancies disappear 
since none of the binary multiplication expressions has the same $\eri$.
Moreover, the distributive law may incur more computations.
For example, there are 2 multiplications and 5 additions in $e$, but 8 multiplications and 7 additions after removing the parentheses.
The detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this paper.

In practice, we only apply distributive law to a constant or loop-invariant scalar variable multiplier.
This may provide more redundancies.
Figure \ref{fig:mgrid}
exhibits a loop in the mgrid benchmark of SPEC2000.
It is a 3D stencil computation code.
The middle one of Figure \ref{fig:mgrid}
shows the code after the redundancy detection with the
second aggressive level.
Note that the code is optimized with the auxiliary array
optimization described above.
$aa\_1\_0$ and $aa\_1\_1$ are auxiliary arrays
found in the second iteration of the do-while loop in the detection algorithm,
and both of them are built by the combination of two $aa\_0\_*$ auxiliary arrays.
There are no more redundancies with this code.
After flattening the expression tree 
using the fourth strategy,
more redundancies are discovered as shown in the right figure.
A new auxiliary array $aa\_3\_0$ is detected in the fourth iteration of the algorithm.



Another set of options can specify the reassociation 
for subtraction and division operations.
For example, $x-y-z$ may produce $x-y$, $x-z$ and $-y-z$.
Thus, it may require a sign change to identify the redundancy
between $y+z$ and $-y-z$.
The rule is simple and just change the first operand to a plus sign
in the $\eri$ calculation.
The division operation can be handled similarly.







\subsection{Detection Algorithm}
\label{subsec:nary-algorithm}

The algorithm on n-ary expression trees
extends the above linear redundancy detection algorithm on binary trees.
Each node in an n-ary tree may have more than two operands, and their
calculation order can be reorganized to eliminate more redundancies.
An expression $e=x\oplus y \oplus\dots$ in the n-ary tree is denoted by \(\oplus(x,y,\cdots)\).

The extension needs to model the conflict relationship
between expressions.
If both $x\oplus y$ and $y\oplus z$ in an expression $\oplus(x,y,z)$
are redundant,
only one of them can belong to the solution.
We define an undirected conflict graph \(G=(V,E)\)
to formalize the constraint. 
Each node in the graph $G$ represents a possible binary expression  $x \oplus y$.
A node and an expression are equivalent in $G$ and used interchangeably.
Since the calculation order can be reorganized, we treat $x \oplus y$ and $y \oplus x$ as the same node.
Each edge indicates the conflict relation between two nodes, which means
that the two expressions (nodes) share the same array reference and cannot be extracted simultaneously.
Thus, any legal solution is an independent set of $G$.

    \[V=\bigcup\limits_{e=\oplus(\dots)}\bigcup\limits_{x,y \in e}\{ x\oplus y \mid x,y \text{ are leaves.}, x \neq y\}\]

    \[E=\{(v,v') \mid v,v' \in V, v=x\oplus y \neq v'=x'\oplus y', \{x,y\} \cap \{x',y'\} \neq \emptyset \}\]


Algorithm \ref{alg:narydetection} presents the extension to 
the linear algorithm for n-ary trees.
The algorithm also follows a similar bottom-up scheme.
It initializes an empty graph $G=(V,E)$ to maintain the
conflict information and updates the graph in the iteration
of the do-while loop.
It is easy to see that the second step in the do-while loop must
process all possible expressions.
In particular, it generates $C_n^2$ 
additional binary expressions for each node with $n$ children and 
calculates their $\eri$ values.
The $\eri$ values of these newly generated binary expressions are computed as they are generated, and their corresponding edges
are added to $G$.
Then, a non-conflicting subset $S$ of expressions
is chosen from $V$ as the solution of redundant computations.
The graph $G$ is updated again by 
removing $S$ and the conflicting nodes in $G$.
The last three steps are the same as Algorithm \ref{alg:lineardetection}.



\begin{algorithm}[t]
  \caption{Detection on n-ary tree}
  \label{alg:narydetection}
  \SetKwRepeat{Do}{do}{while}
 set $\rpi$ of all leaves to $\infty$ \;
  initialize an empty graph $G=(V,E)$\;
  \Do{$\exists$ a leaf $v$ with $\rpi==\infty$}{
    calculate $\rpi$\ for all leaves with $\rpi==\infty$\;
    calculate $\eri$\ for all possible binary expressions whose child's $\rpi$ is just computed\;
    add expressions whose $\eri$ is just computed and the corresponding edges to $G$  \;
    select non-conflicting expression subset $S$ as the redundancy set\;
    remove conflict nodes $\{v| \exists v'\in S, (v,v')\in E\}$ and their edges in $G$\;
    allocate new auxiliary arrays for all redundancies as new leaves \;
    replace redundant expressions  to auxiliary array loads with corresponding offsets  \;
    set the $\rpi$ of new leaves to $\infty$ \;
  }
\end{algorithm}



To determine the optimal solution of the non-conflicting expression subset, an objective function on the graph needs to be defined.
The loop ranges are usually not known at the compiling time.
So it cannot precisely evaluate the redundant computations
between conflict redundancies.
For example, if there are three expressions
$\oplus(x,y,z)$, $\oplus(x',y')$ and $\oplus(y'',z'')$
and $\eri(x\oplus y)=\eri(x'\oplus y')$
and $\eri(y\oplus z)=\eri(y''\oplus z'')$,
it is impossible to determine which one incurs more redundant computations
before the execution.

Therefore, we use an approximate metric.
If $n$ expressions with the same $\eri$ are extracted, the new expression trees have
$n$ less binary expressions that are replaced with auxiliary array loads.
The reduced number of redundant computations on the expression trees can be
approximated to $n-1$, where the minus one denotes the auxiliary array's precomputation.
Let $S$ be a solution and $\eri(S)$ be the set of all $\eri$ values of expressions in $S$, i.e.,
 
  \[\eri(S)=\{\eri(v) \mid v \in S\}.\]
  
The optimal solution in a single iteration is tied to the objective function:
\begin{equation}
    \begin{aligned}
    \argmax_{S \in I_G} |S| - |\eri(S)|
    \end{aligned}
    \label{eq:ori-obj}
\end{equation}
where $I_G$ denotes independent sets of $G$.

This problem can be reduced to the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem by constructing an auxiliary graph $\bar{G}=(\bar{V}, \bar{E})$. 
For each $\eri$ value $k$, $\bar{G}$ adds an auxiliary node $\bar{v}_k$ connected to all nodes with $\eri$ value $k$ in $G$, i.e., $\bar{V}=V \cup V'$ where $V'=\{\bar{v}_k \mid k \in \eri(V)\}, \eri(\bar{v}_k)=k$, 
and $\bar{E}=E \cup \{(\bar{v}_k, v) \mid \bar{v}_k \in V', v \in V, \eri(v)=k\}$.
The formal description is in Theorem~\ref{theorem:MIS}.

\begin{theorem}
    The optimization problem on graph $G$ defined in Equation~\ref{eq:ori-obj}
    can be reduced to the MIS problem on $\bar{G}$.
    \label{theorem:MIS}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
    
    Define $f: I_G \to f(I_G)$ as 
    \[f(S) = S \cup \{\bar{v}_k \in V' \mid k \notin \eri(S)\}.\]
    It's obvious that $\forall S_0,S_1 \in I_G, S_0 \neq S_1 \implies f(S_0) \neq f(S_1)$. So $f$ is injective. The codomain of $f$ is its range $f(I_G)$, so it is surjective. Therefore, $f$ is bijective.

According to the construction of $\bar{G}$,
it's obvious that $\forall \bar{S}\in f(I_G)$, $\bar{S}\in I_{\bar{G}}$, i.e. $f(I_G)\subseteq I_{\bar{G}}$.
Actually $f(I_G)$ is the set of all the independent sets
$\bar{S}$ of $\bar{G}$ such that 
$\eri(\bar{S})=\eri(V)$, i.e., $f(I_G) = \{\bar{S} \in I_{\bar{G}} \mid \eri(\bar{S})=\eri(V)\}$.
On one hand, the function $f$ augments 
any independent set $S\in I_G$ with $\bar{v}_k$  for all $k$ values that are not in $\eri(S)$, thus
we have $\eri(f(S))=\eri(V)$.
On the other hand, given an independent set
$\bar{S}\in I_{\bar{G}}$ such that 
$\eri(\bar{S})=\eri(V)$,
we have $S = \bar{S} \setminus V'$ is 
an independent set of $G$
and $\bar{S} = f(S)\in f(I_G)$.
It's easy to see that 
a MIS $\bar{S}$ of $\bar{G}$
satisfying $\eri(\bar{S})=\eri(V)$, 
thus $f(I_G)$ contains all MIS of $\bar{G}$.

    
    Define objective functions 
    \[ F(S)=|S| + |\eri(V)| - |\eri(S)|, \quad \text{and} \quad \bar{F}(S)=|S|. \] 
    Since $|\eri(V)|$ is a constant given $G$, optimizing $F(S)$ is equivalent to optimizing $F(S) - |\eri(V)|$ which is the objective function in Equation~\ref{eq:ori-obj}, as additive constants do not affect the optimal solution. We now prove that 
    solving the original problem defined by Equation~\ref{eq:ori-obj} ($\argmax_{S \in I_G} F(S)$) on graph $G$ is equivalent to solving the MIS problem ($\argmax_{\bar{S} \in I_{\bar{G}}} \bar{F}(\bar{S})$) on the auxiliary graph $\bar{G}$: 
    
    $f(S)$ adds auxiliary nodes with disappeared $\eri$ values into $S$. So we have
    \begin{equation}
        \begin{aligned}
            \forall S \in I_G,\bar{F}(f(S)) &= |f(S)| \\ 
            &=|S| + |\eri(V)| - |\eri(S)| \\
            &=F(S).
        \end{aligned}
        \label{eq:F-f-trans}
    \end{equation}
    Note that $f$ is proved to be bijective, so it is equivalent to 
    \begin{equation}
        \forall \bar{S} \in f(I_G), \bar{F}(\bar{S})=F(f^{-1}(\bar{S})).
        \label{eq:F-f-inverse-trans}
    \end{equation}

    Since we prove that any MIS of $\bar{G}$ belongs to $f(I_G)$, the objective function for the MIS problem on $\bar{G}$ is equivalent to $\argmax_{\bar{S} \in f(I_G)} \bar{F}(\bar{S})$. Let $\bar{S}^*$ denotes one of the solutions for the MIS problem on $\bar{G}$ and $S^*=f^{-1}(\bar{S}^*)$. Then we have
    \begin{equation*}
        \begin{aligned}
            F(S^*) &= F(f^{-1}(\bar{S}^*)) &&\\ 
            &= \bar{F}(\bar{S}^*) &&\text{(by Equation~\ref{eq:F-f-inverse-trans})} \\ 
            &= \max_{\bar{S} \in f(I_G)} \bar{F}(\bar{S}) &&\text{(because $\bar{S}^*$ is an MIS on $\bar{G}$)} \\
            &= \max_{S \in I_G} \bar{F}(f(S)) &&\text{(replace variable $\bar{S}$ with $f(S)$)} \\
            &= \max_{S \in I_G} F(S) &&\text{(by Equation~\ref{eq:F-f-trans})} .
        \end{aligned}
    \end{equation*}
    So $S^*=\argmax_{S \in I_G} F(S)$.
    Thus, any solution $\bar{S}^*$ for the MIS problem on $\bar{G}$ yields a solution $S^*=f^{-1}(\bar{S}^*)$ for the optimization problem on $G$ defined by Equation~\ref{eq:ori-obj}.
    
\end{proof}

It is well-known that MIS is an NP-hard problem.
For a small number of expressions,
the optimal solution can be found 
by the exhaustive method that enumerates all the possible MIS solutions
within a reasonable time.
However, for loop nests with numerous expressions and operands,
the exhaustive method becomes computationally infeasible within a reasonable time.
We then introduce a heuristic strategy
to reduce the problem size by considering
expressions with specific conditions.

\subsection{Heuristic Strategy}
\label{subsec:dimension-first}


The array's memory access patterns in real applications are typically regular and symmetric. As described in Section~\ref{subsec:optimization}, the auxiliary arrays can be compressed to lower dimensions to save memory and improve the cache performance. Based on the observation, we propose a heuristic algorithm called dimension-first extraction, which aims to find solutions with a higher potential for compression while reducing the problem size. This approach increases the opportunity to leverage cache locality and vectorization. Figure~\ref{fig:mgrid} illustrates how the dimension of auxiliary arrays can be further reduced using the dimension-first extraction method.
For instance, if we choose $R(i-1,k,j)+R(i+1,k,j)$ as an auxiliary array in the first iteration of our algorithm, it cannot be compressed to a one-dimensional array because its reuses are along the $j$ or $k$ dimension. Furthermore, other solutions like $R(i-1,k-1,j)+R(i-1,k,j-1)$ are irregular and may result in discrete memory access, leading to poor locality. In contrast, if $R(i,k,j-1)+R(i,k,j+1)$ is chosen, it can be reused along $i$ dimension.

Dimension-first extraction is a greedy algorithm that prioritizes selecting expressions with zero delta in the innermost dimension, i.e., $e.\mathit{exprDelta}[i_n] = 0$. A zero delta in the innermost dimension indicates that the reuses are more likely to occur along the innermost $i_n$ dimension, as demonstrated in the example in Figure~\ref{fig:mgrid}. 
The algorithm runs in a try-until manner. First, it only generates the nodes with $\mathit{exprDelta}[i_n]=0$ when constructing Delta Graph. This forms a subgraph of the original Delta Graph, containing significantly fewer nodes. If any solutions are found, the algorithm accepts them and returns the control to the Algorithm~\ref{alg:narydetection} to proceed to the next extraction iteration. If no solution is found, the algorithm will generate a new subgraph containing only nodes with $\mathit{exprDelta}[i_{n-1}]=0$ and try to find the solution of this graph, repeating this process until it finds a solution at some dimension $i$.

This algorithm improves the performance of finding the solution by significantly reducing the number of nodes and edges in the Delta Graph. 
Without this algorithm, the mgrid case will generate more than one hundred nodes in the Delta Graph. In practice, the solution for Figure~\ref{fig:mgrid} is found almost immediately with the dimension-first algorithm, whereas the search algorithm may take much longer to find a suboptimal solution.
Additionally, there are multiple solutions satisfying our objective function on the Delta Graph. The dimension-first strategy successfully identifies the innermost loop reuse auxiliary arrays in our experiment, which exhibit better locality and provide opportunities for vectorization.





\section{Experiment}
\label{sec:experiment}
\subsection{Experiment Setup}
We implemented the proposed algorithm framework based on Flang and Clang in LLVM infrastructure. The tool provides options to support different levels of aggressiveness in optimization. Our algorithm performs source-to-source transformations, operating on the AST generated by the compiler frontend. Compilation directives are added before and after the target loops. The performance tests were conducted on two different platforms: an Intel Xeon Gold 6467C 30-core CPU @ 3.40 GHz and an AMD EPYC 9654 96-core Processor @ 2.40 GHz. 
The benchmarks were compiled by gfortran-9.4.0 or gcc-9.4.0 with compilation flags "-O3" to enable all standard optimizations. 

\subsection{Benchmark}

We selected 11 cases in three different applications and 4 stencil kernels to evaluate the performance of the code generated by our tool.
Table~\ref{tab:benchmark} shows the information of the selected cases. All of the loops in the cases are floating-point computations. The column label \textbf{Reduced Ops} represents reduction in run-time arithmetic operations. \textbf{Operations} column contains static analysis of reduced operations, assuming the loop ranges of auxiliary arrays are equivalent to the original loop ranges. Since the reference offsets in the cases are usually small enough, this analysis makes sense and gives some insight about the performance improvement.

POP is a high-performance ocean modeling software used for climate simulation and ocean circulation modeling. WRF is a numerical weather prediction model used for atmospheric research and operational forecasting. mgrid is a benchmark used to simulate multigrid algorithms for solving partial differential equations.
The remaining cases are stencil kernels widely used in scientific applications. \textit{Poisson}, \textit{derivative} and \textit{j3d27pt} are 3D stencil kernels whose grid size is set to $100^3$ in our experiment, while \textit{gaussian} are 2D stencil kernels with grid size set to $500^2$. 
The POP and WRF kernels were evaluated using their official implementations in the SPEC CPU 2017 benchmark suite, while the mgrid kernel was executed through the SPEC CPU 2000 framework, with all SPEC tests adhering to prescribed input sets and execution rules.

Our algorithm is effective to find various redundant arithmetic operations. The $\sin/\cos$ operations are reduced from $16$ to only $4$ in case \textit{calc\_tpoints} of POP. A large number of auxiliary arrays are found in WRF's cases without much iterations, and the operations are reduced in nearly half. RACE can also handle very large expressions, such as the \textit{derivative} case, where 81 auxiliary arrays are found and the multiplications are reduced from $297$ to $101$.

The detection algorithm on n-ary tree is important to find more redundancies.
If only the redundancy detection algorithm on binary trees is used, the case \textit{diffusion1} and \textit{diffusion2} can only identify 8 and 9 auxiliary arrays, respectively, with a reduction of 8 and 11 redundant operations. In contrast, using the detection algorithm on an n-ary tree allows for the identification of 20 and 19 auxiliary arrays, with a reduction of 25 and 26 redundant calculations, respectively.

In case \textit{rprj3}, the loop variables inside the array subscripts are preceded by a multiplication factor of 2. Although the names of the array references in it are the same, they have different $\rpi$ value. The redundancies are successfully found, which shows the effectiveness of our two level hash algorithm.
  
\subsection{Results}

\begin{figure}[h!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{fig/Intel.pdf}
  \caption{The speedup of different optimization methods relative to the original code on the Intel CPU. Among the legend, RACE-NR refers to the use of our algorithm without reassociation; RACE uses the full abilities which involve reassociation, dimension-first heuristic extraction, and array contraction. Note that the ESR method uses reassociation.}
  \label{fig:perf-intel}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[h!]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{fig/AMD.pdf}
  \caption{The speedup of different optimization methods relative to the original code on the AMD CPU. The legend is the same as in Figure~\ref{fig:perf-intel}.}
  \label{fig:perf-amd}
\end{figure}

We evaluated the single-core performance of the code generated by our tool compared to the baseline (original) code. Since our algorithm targets loop-level optimization, we report the loop-level speedup. Figure~\ref{fig:perf-intel} and Figure~\ref{fig:perf-amd} show the performance speedup on the Intel and AMD CPUs, respectively.

Our results demonstrate that RACE achieves significant performance improvements across most benchmarks. RACE outperforms ESR in 14 out of 15 cases on both platforms, except for the \textit{ocn\_export} case where RACE generates the same code as ESR. 
The RACE-NR method, despite not using reassociation, still provides notable improvements in cases like \textit{calc\_tpoints}, \textit{derivative} etc.
The ESR method, while effective in some cases, does not achieve the same level of speedup as RACE, highlighting the additional benefits of the full RACE algorithm. The ESR method exhibited several negative optimizations. This is because the auxiliary variables extracted by ESR are scalars placed in the innermost loop and reused in a pipeline manner, which hinders the compiler's vectorization optimization. RACE can keep the auxiliary arrays in multi-dimensional arrays, which facilitates vectorization. 

The overall performance gain is influenced by the redundancies detected by our algorithm, as detailed in Table~\ref{tab:benchmark}. Fewer auxiliary arrays are found in the case of \textit{rhs\_ph} compared to those in the \textit{diffusion} case, which explains why the speedup for \textit{rhs\_ph} is lower than that for \textit{diffusion}. A lot of redundant operations are found in the \textit{derivative} case, up to 81 auxiliary arrays and 196 reduced multiplications, which lead to a significant speedup on both platforms. The intensity of arithmetic operations largely affects the benefits of reducing redundant computations. The performance speedup on the Intel CPU reaches 3.06x in the \textit{calc\_tpoints} case of POP, where the $\sin/\cos$ functions are arithmetic-intensive. This pattern also holds for the case \textit{ocn\_export}, where the reduced operations are not many but the speedup is notable.
Cases in mgrid and stencil kernels involve many array references with the same name, leading to multiple solutions when solving the optimal reuse problem defined in Section~\ref{subsec:nary-algorithm}. The heuristic strategy proposed in Section~\ref{subsec:dimension-first} identifies the auxiliary arrays with innermost loop reuse, which are more cache-friendly. 

However, for loops that are memory-access intensive, such as the \textit{rprj3} case, the optimization is less effective. Moreover, reducing the intensity of arithmetic operations may increase the memory pressure. While auxiliary arrays reduce arithmetic operations, they introduce additional memory allocation and expand the memory access address space. The newly allocated arrays increase the cache working set, possibly leading to more cache misses. Compressing the dimensions of the auxiliary arrays using the method proposed in Section~\ref{subsec:optimization} mitigates this issue.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This paper proposes RACE, which defines a two-level hashing algorithm to detect redundant array computations in nested loops. The first-level hash uses $\rpi$ to determine whether two array references share the same memory access pattern. 
The second-level hash computes $\eri$ for each binary expression as an attribute within the expression, which encodes the expression-level reuse without explicitly comparing two different expressions.
A linear-time detection algorithm for binary expression trees is proposed based on $\eri$. After extraction, code generation and optimization of the auxiliary arrays are discussed.

Furthermore, tree flattening and the Delta Graph are introduced to identify redundancies in n-ary trees. The objective function for optimal single-iteration redundancy elimination is defined using the Delta Graph, which is reduced to a maximum independent set (MIS) problem. To accelerate the solution of this problem, a memory-friendly heuristic algorithm is presented to identify auxiliary arrays with inner-loop reuse.

Experiments show that our algorithm achieves significant speedups on various benchmarks, and the effectiveness of the detection algorithm for n-ary trees and the dimension-first heuristic strategy is demonstrated.

title: Modular functors from conformal blocks of rational vertex operator algebras
summary:
For a vertex operator algebra $V$, one may naturally define spaces of
conformal blocks following a construction of Frenkel--Ben-Zvi generalized by
Damiolini--Gibney--Tarasca. If $V$ is strongly rational, these spaces of
conformal blocks form vector bundles over a suitable moduli space of algebraic
curves. In this article, we establish, under the same assumptions, the widely
expected topological result that the spaces of conformal blocks produce a
modular functor, i.e. a modular algebra over an extension of the surface
operad. This entails that the category $\mathcal{C}_V$ of admissible
$V$-modules inherits from the topology a ribbon Grothendieck--Verdier structure
that leads even to the structure of a modular fusion category whose structure
comes directly from the spaces of conformal blocks of $V$. As a direct
consequence, we prove that the modular functor from conformal blocks extends to
a three-dimensional topological field theory and comes with a description in
terms of factorization homology.

summary:
We have performed hyperfine spectroscopy of two transitions in ground-state
deuterium and searched for violations of \CPT and Lorentz symmetry that would
manifest as sidereal variations of the observed transition frequencies. Several
non-relativistic proton coefficients of the Standard-Model Extension framework
have been addressed. The spin-independent coefficients with momentum power
$k$=2,4 are constrained for the first time. Bounds on spin-dependent
coefficients are improved by exploiting a sensitivity enhancement originating
from the relative momenta of the nucleons in the deuteron. The best previous
constraints by hydrogen maser measurements are surpassed by 4 and 14 orders of
magnitude for coefficients with $k$=2 and 4, respectively. Furthermore, we find
a deuterium zero-field hyperfine splitting of \SI{327.3843549(0.0000028)}{\mega
\hertz}. This is in agreement with the literature and presents the most precise
in-beam measurement of this quantity.

title: Modeling active nematics via the nematic locking principle
summary:
Active nematic systems consist of rod-like internally driven subunits that
interact with one another to form large-scale coherent flows. They are
important examples of far-from-equilibrium fluids, which exhibit a wealth of
nonlinear behavior. This includes active turbulence, in which topological
defects braid around one another in a chaotic fashion. One of the most studied
examples of active nematics is a dense two-dimensional layer of microtubules,
crosslinked by kinesin molecular motors that inject extensile deformations into
the fluid. Though numerous studies have modeled microtubule-based active
nematics, no consensus has emerged on how to fully capture the features of the
experimental system. To better understand the foundations for modeling this
system, we propose a fundamental principle we call the nematic locking
principle: individual microtubules cannot rotate without all neighboring
microtubules also rotating. Physically, this is justified by the high density
of the microtubules, their elongated nature, and their corresponding steric
interactions. We assert that nematic locking holds throughout the majority of
the material but breaks down in the neighborhood of topological defects and
other regions of low density. We derive the most general nematic transport
equation consistent with this principle and also derive the most general term
that violates it. We examine the standard Beris-Edwards approach used to model
this system and show that it violates nematic locking throughout the majority
of the material. We then propose a modification to the Beris-Edwards model that
enforces nematic locking nearly everywhere. This modification shuts off
fracturing except in regions where the order parameter is reduced. The
resulting simulations show strong nematic locking throughout the bulk of the
material, consistent with experimental observation.

title: SparStencil: Retargeting Sparse Tensor Cores to Scientific Stencil Computations via Structured Sparsity Transformation
summary:
Sparse Tensor Cores offer exceptional performance gains for AI workloads by
exploiting structured 2:4 sparsity. However, their potential remains untapped
for core scientific workloads such as stencil computations, which exhibit
irregular sparsity patterns.This paper presents SparStencil, the first system
to retarget sparse TCUs for scientific stencil computations through structured
sparsity transformation. SparStencil introduces three key techniques: (1)
Adaptive Layout Morphing, which restructures stencil patterns into
staircase-aligned sparse matrices via a flatten-and-crush pipeline; (2)
Structured Sparsity Conversion, which formulates transformation as a graph
matching problem to ensure compatibility with 2:4 sparsity constraints; (3)
Automatic Kernel Generation, which compiles transformed stencils into optimized
sparse MMA kernels via layout search and table-driven memory mapping. Evaluated
on 79 stencil kernels spanning diverse scientific domains, SparStencil achieves
up to 7.1x speedup (3.1x on average) over state-of-the-art framework while
reducing code complexity and matching or exceeding expert-tuned performance in
both compute throughput and memory efficiency.

bib.abstract: While Tensor Core Units (TCUs) excel in AI tasks, their application to HPC algorithms like stencil computations faces significant challenges due to sparsity, which leads to underutilization and exacerbates memory-bound limitations. This paper introduces FlashFFTStencil1, a memory-efficient stencil computing system designed to bridge FFT to fully-dense stencil computations on TCUs. Aimed at bound shifting, FlashFFTStencil comprises three key techniques: Kernel Tailoring on HBM fuses distinct kernels to enhance parallelism while reducing memory transfer and footprint; Architecture Aligning on SMEM restructures FFT-based stencil computations into dense matrix multiplications tailored for shared memory architecture; Computation Streamlining on TCU optimizes TCU utilization and thread parallelism by minimizing pipeline stalls and maximizing register reuse. Notably, a distinctive extension is FlashFFTStencil's ability to enable theoretically unrestricted temporal fusion by FFT. Results show that FlashFFTStencil achieves effective sparsity-free bound shifting, with an average speedup of 2.57x over the state-of-the-art. FlashFFTStencil pioneers a new era in unifying computational patterns within the HPC landscape and bridges them with cutting-edge AI-driven hardware innovations like TCUs.

bib.abstract: Stencil computations play a pivotal role in numerous scientific and industrial applications, yet their efficient execution on specialized hardware accelerators like Tensor Core Units (TCUs) remains a challenge. This paper introduces LoRAStencil1, a novel stencil computing system designed to mitigate memory access redundancies on TCUs through low-rank adaptation. We first identify a nuanced form of this redundancy, dimension residue, specific to TCUs. Then LoRAStencil leverages orchestrated mathematical transformations to decompose stencil weight matrices into smaller rank-1 matrices, facilitating efficient data gathering along residual dimensions. It comprises three key components: memory-efficient Residual Dimension Gathering to facilitate more data reuse, compute-saving Pyramidal Matrix Adaptation to exploit the inherent low-rank characteristics, and performance-boosting Butterfly Vector Swapping to circumvent all data shuffles. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that LoRAStencil address dimension residues effectively, which outperforms state-of-the-arts with up to a 2.16x speedup, offering promising advancements for efficient tensorized stencil computation on TCUs by Low-Rank Adaptation.
bib.title: { LoRAStencil: Low-Rank Adaptation of Stencil Computation on Tensor Cores }

bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 29th ACM SIGPLAN Annual Symposium on Principles and Practice of Parallel Programming
bib.abstract: Tensor Core Unit (TCU) is increasingly integrated into modern high-performance processors to enhance matrix multiplication performance. However, constrained to its over-specification, its potential for improving other critical scientific operations like stencil computations remains untapped.This paper presents ConvStencil1, a novel stencil computing system designed to efficiently transform stencil computation to matrix multiplication on Tensor Cores. We first develop a performance model for ConvStencil to guide algorithm design and optimization on TCUs. Based on this model, we propose three techniques: (1) Memory-efficient Layout Transformation using the stencil2row method; (2) Computation-dense Compute Adaptation with Dual Tessellation and kernel fusion; and (3) Performance-boosting Conflict Removal using a Lookup Table and Dirty Bits Padding. ConvStencil outperforms other stencil optimization frameworks, achieving significant speedups compared to solutions like AMOS, cuDNN, Brick, DRStencil, and TCStencil. By transforming stencil computation on Tensor Cores, ConvStencil promises to improve the performance of various scientific and engineering applications.
bib.title: ConvStencil: Transform Stencil Computation to Matrix Multiplication on Tensor Cores
bib.author: Chen, Yuetao and Li, Kun and Wang, Yuhao and Bai, Donglin and Wang, Lei and Ma, Lingxiao and Yuan, Liang and Zhang, Yunquan and Cao, Ting and Yang, Mao

bib.keywords: GPU, convolution, stencil, systolic array, CUDA
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis
bib.abstract: This paper proposes a versatile high-performance execution model, inspired by systolic arrays, for memory-bound regular kernels running on CUDA-enabled GPUs. We formulate a systolic model that shifts partial sums by CUDA warp primitives for the computation. We also employ register files as a cache resource in order to operate the entire model efficiently. We demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of the proposed model for a wide variety of stencil kernels that appear commonly in HPC, and also convolution kernels (increasingly important in deep learning workloads). Our algorithm outperforms the top reported state-of-the-art stencil implementations, including implementations with sophisticated temporal and spatial blocking techniques, on the two latest Nvidia architectures: Tesla V100 and P100. For 2D convolution of general filter sizes and shapes, our algorithm is on average 2.5\texttimes{} faster than Nvidia's NPP on V100 and P100 GPUs.
bib.title: A Versatile Software Systolic Execution Model for GPU Memory-Bound Kernels
bib.author: Chen, Peng and Wahib, Mohamed and Takizawa, Shinichiro and Takano, Ryousei and Matsuoka, Satoshi

bib.keywords: Box Stencil, Tessellation, Stencil Computation, Star Stencil
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 48th International Conference on Parallel Processing
bib.abstract: Stencil computations represent a very common class of nested loops in scientific and engineering applications. The exhaustively studied tiling is one of the most powerful transformation techniques to explore the data locality and parallelism. Existing work often uniformly handles different stencil shapes. This paper first presents a concept called natural block to identify the difference between the star and box stencils. Then we propose anew two-level tessellation scheme for star stencils, where the natural block, as well as its successors can tessellate the spatial space and their extensions along the time dimension are able to form a tessellation of the iteration space. Furthermore, a novel implementation technique called double updating is developed for star stencils specifically to improve the in-core data reuse pattern. Evaluation results are provided that demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.
bib.title: Tessellating Star Stencils
bib.author: Yuan, Liang and Huang, Shan and Zhang, Yunquan and Cao, Hang

bib.keywords: stencil computation, tiling, tessellation
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis
bib.abstract: Stencil computations represent a very common class of nested loops in scientific and engineering applications. The exhaustively studied tiling is one of the most powerful transformation techniques to explore the data locality and parallelism. Unlike previous work, which mostly blocks the iteration space of a stencil directly, this paper proposes a novel two-level tessellation scheme. A set of blocks are designed to tessellate the spatial space in various ways. The blocks can be processed in parallel without redundant computation. This corresponds to extending them along the time dimension and can form a tessellation of the iteration space. Experimental results show that our code performs up to 12% better than the existing highly concurrent schemes for the 3d27p stencil.
bib.title: Tessellating Stencils
bib.author: Yuan, Liang and Zhang, Yunquan and Guo, Peng and Huang, Shan

bib.keywords: vectorization, stencil, compiler optimization
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis
bib.abstract: Stencil computations in real-world scientific applications may contain multiple interrelated stencils, have multiple input grids, and use higher order discretizations with high arithmetic intensity and complex expression structures. In combination, these properties place immense demands on the memory hierarchy that limit performance. Blocking techniques like tiling are used to exploit reuse in caches. Additional fine-grain data blocking can also reduce TLB, hardware prefetch, and cache pressure.In this paper, we present a code generation approach designed to further improve tiled stencil performance by exploiting reuse within the block, increasing instruction-level parallelism, and exposing opportunities for the backend compiler to eliminate redundant computation. It also enables efficient vector code generation for CPUs and GPUs. For a wide range of complex stencil computations, we are able to achieve substantial speedups over tiled baselines for the Intel KNL, Intel Skylake-X, and NVIDIA P100 architectures.
bib.title: Exploiting Reuse and Vectorization in Blocked Stencil Computations on CPUs and GPUs
bib.author: Zhao, Tuowen and Basu, Protonu and Williams, Samuel and Hall, Mary and Johansen, Hans

bib.keywords: overlapped tiling, stencil, gpu, opencl
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 26th ACM International Conference on Supercomputing
bib.abstract: Stencil computations arise in many scientific computing domains, and often represent time-critical portions of applications. There is significant interest in offloading these computations to high-performance devices such as GPU accelerators, but these architectures offer challenges for developers and compilers alike. Stencil computations in particular require careful attention to off-chip memory access and the balancing of work among compute units in GPU devices.In this paper, we present a code generation scheme for stencil computations on GPU accelerators, which optimizes the code by trading an increase in the computational workload for a decrease in the required global memory bandwidth. We develop compiler algorithms for automatic generation of efficient, time-tiled stencil code for GPU accelerators from a high-level description of the stencil operation. We show that the code generation scheme can achieve high performance on a range of GPU architectures, including both nVidia and AMD devices.
bib.title: High-Performance Code Generation for Stencil Computations on GPU Architectures
bib.author: Holewinski, Justin and Pouchet, Louis-No\"{e}l and Sadayappan, P.

bib.keywords: stencil computations, tiling, GPGPU, resource management
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 9th Annual Workshop on General Purpose Processing Using Graphics Processing Unit
bib.abstract: GPUs are an attractive target for data parallel stencil computations prevalent in scientific computing and image processing applications. Many tiling schemes, such as overlapped tiling and split tiling, have been proposed in past to improve the performance of stencil computations. While effective for 2D stencils, these techniques do not achieve the desired improvements for 3D stencils due to the hardware constraints of GPU.A major challenge in optimizing stencil computations is to effectively utilize all resources available on the GPU. In this paper we develop a tiling strategy that makes better use of resources like shared memory and register file available on the hardware. We present a systematic methodology to reason about which strategy should be employed for a given stencil and also discuss implementation choices that have a significant effect on the achieved performance. Applying these techniques to various 2D and 3D stencils gives a performance improvement of 200-400% over existing tools that target such computations.
bib.title: Effective Resource Management for Enhancing Performance of 2D and 3D Stencils on GPUs

bib.abstract: Popular high-order schemes with compact stencils for Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) include Discontinuous Galerkin (DG), Spectral Difference (SD), and Spectral Volume (SV) methods. The recently proposed Flux Reconstruction (FR) approach or Correction Procedure using Reconstruction (CPR) is based on a differential formulation and provides a unifying framework for these high-order schemes. Here we present a brief review of recent progress in FR/CPR research as well as some pacing items and future challenges.

bib.abstract:
OpenSBLI is an open-source code-generation system for compressible fluid dynamics (CFD) on heterogeneous computing architectures. Written in Python, OpenSBLI is an explicit high-order finite-difference solver on structured curvilinear meshes. Shock-capturing is performed by a choice of high-order Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) or Targeted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (TENO) schemes. OpenSBLI generates a complete CFD solver in the Oxford Parallel Structured (OPS) domain specific language. The OPS library is embedded in C code, enabling massively-parallel execution of the code on a variety of high-performance-computing architectures, including GPUs. The present paper presents a code base that has been completely rewritten from the earlier proof of concept Jacobs et al. (2017) [7], allowing shock capturing, coordinate transformations for complex geometries, and a wide range of boundary conditions, including solid walls with and without heat transfer. A suite of validation and verification cases are presented, plus demonstration of a large-scale Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of a transitional Shockwave Boundary Layer Interaction (SBLI). The code is shown to have good weak and strong scaling on multi-GPU clusters. We demonstrate that code-generation and domain specific languages are suitable for performing efficient large-scale simulations of complex fluid flows on emerging computing architectures.
Program summary
Program Title: OpenSBLI code-generation framework for compressible fluid dynamics on heterogeneous architectures CPC Library link to program files: https://doi.org/10.17632/3sdb6hck2c.1 Developer's repository link: https://github.com/opensbli/opensbli Licensing provisions: GPLv3 Programming languages: Python, C/C++, OPS DSL Nature of problem: The compressible 3D Navier-Stokes equations are solved via Implicit Large Eddy Simulation (ILES) or Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS). Solution method: OpenSBLI [1,2] is a Python-based code-generation system that uses symbolic algebra to generate a complete CFD solver in C/C++. The basic algorithm is a stencil-based finite-difference solver on structured curvilinear meshes. Shock-capturing is performed by a selection of high-order Weighted/Targeted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO/TENO) schemes. Explicit low-storage Runge-Kutta schemes are used for time-advancement. Additional comments including restrictions and unusual features: The generated code is compliant with the Oxford Parallel Structured (OPS) [3] software library. OpenSBLI/OPS executables can be generated for the OpenMP, MPI, CUDA, OpenCL, and OpenACC parallel programming paradigms. Multi-GPU support is available via combinations of MPI with CUDA, OpenCL or OpenACC.
